title: Homer's epic heroes were everyday names for ordinary Mycenaeans
dek: On the accounting tablets from Mycenaean palaces, Eteocles and Achilles were merely the names of commoners who owed goods to the crown—the "heroic" names from Homer's epics were actually everyday names anyone bore then.
why: The question of whether Agamemnon was real spans the entire episode, only answered directly by the guest at the end.
who: Anyone curious about the Trojan War and Homer's sources, and how archaeological evidence revises our memory of myth.
skip: The sections on Mycenaean women and children have sparse evidence; the guest himself admits knowing little about them, so you can skip ahead.

points.h: "Mycenaean" is a modern label, not what they called themselves
points.body: The term "Mycenaean" was coined by modern scholars using the name of the Mycenae site. The people themselves are called Achaeans or Danaans in Homer's epics. How they actually referred to themselves remains unknown; Linear B tablets reveal only how certain place names were written then.

points.h: A federation of independent states, not one unified Mycenaean empire
points.body: Mycenaean civilization was not a unified empire but a collection of independent kingdoms: Pylos, Mycenae, Argos, Thebes, and others. They shared language and religious beliefs, but remained politically separate. While Mycenae sat strategically between Argos and Tiryns and Egypt's artifacts have been found there, suggesting regional dominance, there is no evidence for a "king of kings" like Agamemnon.

points.h: Crete's shift to Linear B may have been cultural adoption, not conquest
points.body: Around 1450 BCE, Linear A on Crete was replaced by Linear B (the Mycenaean script), and burial styles shifted to mainland "warrior graves" with swords and helmets. The standard assumption is military invasion, but Crete's elite may simply have adopted continental customs and weaponry. No written records document an actual conquest.

points.h: Tablet records show "heroes" were simply common people's names
points.body: Mycenaean palace tablets primarily recorded mundane transactions: how many sheep or goats villagers owed the crown. Yet these mundane records contain the names Eteocles and Achilles—the very heroes of Homer's epics—proving these "heroic" names were ordinary labels anyone could bear. The tablets even mention one real "Smith" who made bronze tools professionally.

points.h: Cyclopean walls were oversized by design: built to intimidate, not defend
points.body: The "Cyclopean" fortifications at Mycenae and Tiryns were built with massive stones, seven to eight meters thick—far exceeding what actual defense required. Later Greek writers like Pausanias refused to believe mortals could build them, attributing them to mythical giants. The walls were meant to awe and intimidate. The passage before the Lion Gate was enclosed on three sides to create a killing zone where archers could fire down on attackers.

points.h: Agamemnon was likely a composite memory, not a historical person
points.body: Asked directly whether Agamemnon was real, Kershaw gave a blunt answer: probably not. He likely represents a vague folk memory of some powerful ruler, projected backward in time—similar to how the mythological Eurystheus may have a historical kernel. Myth preserves not what actually happened, but a version of the past crafted to justify the present.

points.h: When Mycenaean palaces fell, the people remained—only the system collapsed
points.body: Around 1200 BCE, Mycenaean palaces throughout the region were destroyed in succession. Yet this did not mean the population vanished. People continued to live at Mycenae, Tiryns, and elsewhere; they even contributed soldiers when Persia invaded Greece five centuries later. What truly disappeared was the palace-centered administration and the use of writing. The language itself—early Greek—never broke the chain of transmission.

points.h: Bronze Age collapse was systemic: the whole structure fell when one piece broke
points.body: Scholars have proposed many causes for Mycenaean collapse: earthquakes, climate change, plague, invasions by the Sea Peoples. None is definitively proven by archaeology. A more widely accepted explanation is systemic collapse—the civilization was built like a tower of blocks so interdependent that removing any single crucial support brought the entire structure down.
